html:
Denmark-Norway was the joint realm of the kingdoms of Denmark and Norway under one king in Copenhagen, from the end of the Kalmar Union in the 1520s until 1814. It also took in Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, and its king also ruled the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein. The map uses the name for Danish and Norwegian lands from 1000 onward, long before the union was formed.

The two crowns had shared a king since 1380. After Sweden left the Kalmar Union in 1523, Denmark and Norway stayed together, and in 1536 Norway lost its own council and was ruled from Copenhagen. In the same years the king brought in the Lutheran Reformation.

Some points in its history:

  • Long wars with Sweden for control of the Baltic. In 1658 Denmark lost Scania, the southern tip of today's Sweden.
  • In 1660 the king made himself an absolute monarch.
  • Small colonies abroad: Tranquebar in India, forts on the Gold Coast of Africa, and the Danish West Indies, sugar islands worked by enslaved Africans brought in the Atlantic slave trade. From 1721 the missionary Hans Egede renewed Danish ties with Greenland.
  • Norway supplied timber, fish and sailors, and Danish became the written language of both countries.

In the Napoleonic Wars Britain bombarded Copenhagen in 1807 and seized the fleet, pushing Denmark to Napoleon's side. Defeat followed, and by the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 Denmark gave Norway to Sweden, creating Sweden-Norway. Denmark kept Iceland, the Faroes and Greenland.
